hints: Resolve perpendicular to the $20^\circ$ inclined plane to find the normal reaction: $R = 15g\cos 20^\circ$.
Calculate the maximum limiting friction force: $F = \mu R = 0.2(15g\cos 20^\circ)$.
The least possible $X$ occurs when the particle is on the point of slipping down the plane, so friction acts up the plane: $X_{\min} + F = 15g\sin 20^\circ$.
The greatest possible $X$ occurs when the particle is on the point of slipping up the plane, so friction acts down the plane: $X_{\max} = 15g\sin 20^\circ + F$.
walkthrough:
Resolve forces perpendicular to the inclined plane in equilibrium to find the normal reaction $R$:
$$R = mg\cos 20^\circ = 15(10)\cos 20^\circ = 150\cos 20^\circ \approx 140.95\text{ N}$$

Calculate the maximum limiting friction force $F$ using $F = \mu R$ with $\mu = 0.2$:
$$F = \mu R = 0.2 \times 140.95 = 28.19\text{ N}$$

Calculate the component of weight acting down the incline:
$$W_\parallel = mg\sin 20^\circ = 150\sin 20^\circ \approx 51.30\text{ N}$$

For the least possible value of $X$, the particle is about to slip downwards, so friction acts up the plane:
$$X_{\min} + F = W_\parallel \implies X_{\min} = 51.30 - 28.19 = 23.1\text{ N}$$

For the greatest possible value of $X$, the particle is about to slip upwards, so friction acts down the plane:
$$X_{\max} = W_\parallel + F = 51.30 + 28.19 = 79.5\text{ N}$$

teacher_walkthrough:
First, resolve forces perpendicular to the inclined plane. The normal reaction $R$ balances the perpendicular component of the particle's weight:
$$R = mg\cos\theta = 15 \times 10 \times \cos 20^\circ = 150\cos 20^\circ$$
$$R = 150 \times 0.939693 \approx 140.954\text{ N}$$

Calculate the maximum available limiting friction between the particle and the surface using $F_{\max} = \mu R$ with $\mu = 0.2$:
$$F_{\max} = 0.2 \times 140.954 = 28.191\text{ N}$$

Calculate the downward component of weight acting along the line of greatest slope:
$$W_\parallel = mg\sin 20^\circ = 150\sin 20^\circ = 150 \times 0.342020 \approx 51.303\text{ N}$$
The pulling force $X$ acts up the plane. The particle remains stationary as long as friction can prevent motion.

Case 1 (Least value of $X$): If $X$ is at its minimum, the particle is on the verge of sliding down the slope, so friction acts up the slope to support $X$:
$$X_{\min} + F_{\max} = W_\parallel$$
$$X_{\min} + 28.191 = 51.303$$
$$X_{\min} = 51.303 - 28.191 = 23.112\text{ N} \approx 23.1\text{ N}$$

Case 2 (Greatest value of $X$): If $X$ is at its maximum, the particle is on the verge of sliding up the slope, so friction acts down the slope opposing $X$:
$$X_{\max} = W_\parallel + F_{\max}$$
$$X_{\max} = 51.303 + 28.191 = 79.494\text{ N} \approx 79.5\text{ N}$$
